Summary:

Fallah and colleagues characterize the connectivity between two basal ganglia output nuclei, the SNr and GPe, and a the pedunculopontine nucleus, a brainstem nucleus that is part of the mesencephalic locomotor region. Through a series of systematic electrophysiological studies, they find that these regions target and inhibit different populations of neurons, with anatomical organization. Overall, SNr projects to PPN and inhibits all major cell types, while the GPe inhibits glutamatergic and GABAergic PPN neurons, and preferentially in the caudal part of the nucleus. Optogenetic manipulation of these inputs in the had opposing effects on behavior - SNr terminals in the PPN drove place aversion, while GPe terminals drove place preference.

Strengths:

This work is thorough and systematic characterization of a set of relatively understudied circuits. They build on the classic notions of basal ganglia connectivity and suggest a number of interesting future directions to dissect motor control and valence processing in brainstem systems.

Limitations:

All the cell type recording studies showing subtle differences in the degree of inhibition and anatomical organization of that inhibition suggest a complex effect of general optogenetic manipulation of SNr or GPe terminals in the PPN. It will be important to determine if SNr or GPe inputs onto a particular cell type in PPN are more or less critical for the how the locomotion and valence effects demonstrated here.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.102308.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.102308.3.sa3)

The study by Fallah et al. provides a thorough characterization of the effects of two basal ganglia output pathways, the SNr and the GPe, on cholinergic, glutamatergic, and GABAergic neurons of the PPN. Using a combination of optogenetics-assisted electrophysiology and behavioral assays in genetically defined mouse lines, the authors show that SNr projections broadly inhibit all PPN subtypes along the rostrocaudal axis, whereas GPe projections are mostly restricted to the caudal PPN and predominantly target glutamatergic neurons, with a lesser effect on GABAergic neurons. Activation of these inputs in vivo revealed opposing behavioral effects: SNr stimulation increased locomotion and caused avoidance in the real-time place preference (RTPP) task, while GPe stimulation reduced locomotion and increased time spent in the stimulation zone.

Strengths:

The evidence for functional connectivity between SNr and GPe inputs and specific PPN cell types is solid and highlights a prominent influence of SNr across the PPN. The identification of a GPe projection that selectively targets caudal glutamatergic PPN neurons is unexpected and highly relevant to understanding basal ganglia-brainstem interactions. The study stands out for its systematic cell-type-specific approach and the combination of electrophysiological and behavioral data. Importantly, the authors addressed key concerns from the initial review by performing new analyses and adding important controls:

Motor activity was re-analyzed at higher temporal resolution, revealing more nuanced effects of stimulation (Fig. S2).

The concern that motor effects might confound RTPP performance was mitigated by analyzing unstimulated test sessions, which showed that place preference or aversion persisted in the absence of stimulation (Fig. 7G).

The potential recruitment of SNc dopaminergic projections was directly tested using DAT-Cre mice, confirming that dopaminergic axon stimulation drives locomotion and reward but does not explain the aversive effect seen with broader SNr activation (Fig. S3).

Weaknesses:

While the revised analyses and added data strengthen the conclusions, the interpretation of the behavioral effects remains somewhat limited by the use of RTPP, which can be influenced by motor changes, even with unilateral stimulation. Nonetheless, the additional controls and thorough discussion now acknowledge and address these caveats appropriately.

Some minor clarifying edits would enhance the manuscript's precision and readability, including improvements to terminology, data presentation, figure referencing, and the organization of behavioral and statistical reporting.

Conclusion:

This is a strong and compelling study that provides a detailed and novel characterization of basal ganglia inputs to the PPN and their behavioral relevance. The authors were responsive to reviewer feedback, and the revised manuscript is significantly improved. The findings advance our understanding of how basal ganglia output pathways engage brainstem circuits to modulate locomotion and valence.

claims.claim: There was no difference in amplitude of the first oIPSC in the stimulus train between rostral vs caudal cholinergic neurons.
claims.source: There was no difference in amplitude of the first oIPSC in the stimulus train between rostral vs caudal cholinergic neurons (mean ± SEM; first oIPSC n=15 Rostral: 92.6±18 pA, n=20 Caudal: 115.2±17 pA; unpaired t-test, t=0.9041, df = 33, CI –28.4–73.7, p=0.3725; p=0.3725; Figure 2E and F).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data comparing rostral and caudal neurons.

claims.claim: The paired-pulse ratio (PPR) of the peak of the first two currents in the stimulation train did not differ between rostral and caudal cholinergic neurons.
claims.source: In addition, the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) of the peak of the first two currents in the stimulation train did not differ (mean ± SEM; PPR n=15 Rostral: 0.96±0.04, n=20 Caudal: 0.97±0.05; unpaired t-test, t=0.1082, df = 33, CI –0.13–0.14, p=0.9145; Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data comparing short-term synaptic plasticity.

claims.claim: SNr synaptic inputs onto cholinergic neurons do not undergo significant short-term synaptic plasticity in either the rostral or caudal PPN.
claims.source: SNr synaptic inputs onto cholinergic neurons do not undergo significant short-term synaptic plasticity in either the rostral or caudal PPN.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of normalized current amplitudes and paired-pulse ratios from electrophysiological recordings.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference between the percent frequency change in rostral and caudal cholinergic neurons during SNr axon stimulation.
claims.source: However, there was no significant difference between the percent frequency change in rostral and caudal neurons during SNr axon stimulation (mean ± SEM; %Frequency n=14 Rostral: During Stimulation 35.62 ± 8.87%, Post Stimulation 136.1 ± 7.803%; n=23 Caudal: During Stimulation 52.11 ± 8.43%, Post Stimulation 119.1 ± 4.614%; two-way ANOVA, StimulationF(1, 35)=81.9 p<0.0001, RegionF(1, 35)=0.002052 p=0.9641, InteractionF(1, 35)=3.273 p=0.0790; Figure 2K)
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of firing frequency changes during optogenetic stimulation.

claims.claim: Rostral cholinergic neurons had greater rebound activity compared with caudal cholinergic neurons.
claims.source: However, rostral cholinergic neurons had greater rebound activity compared with caudal cholinergic neurons as measured by the absolute change in rebound frequency [median (IQR); ΔRebFrq n=14 Rostral: 1.64 Hz (1.00–2.17 Hz), n=22 Caudal: 0.83 Hz (0.42–1.14 Hz); Mann Whitney, U=79, p=0.0142; Figure 2M].
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of rebound firing frequency after inhibition.

claims.claim: There is a weak but significant negative correlation between the frequency decrease during SNr axon stimulation and the rebound frequency increase in cholinergic PPN neurons.
claims.source: We found a weak but significant negative correlation between the frequency decrease during SNr axon stimulation and the rebound frequency increase (Spearman r=−0.372, p=0.039, Figure 2N and O).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: All rostral GABAergic PPN neurons (12/12) received inhibitory input from the SNr.
claims.source: We found that all rostral (n=12/12, N=6) and most caudal (n=20/22, N=6) recorded GABAergic PPN neurons received inhibitory input from the SNr (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological recordings showing connectivity between SNr and GABAergic PPN neurons.

claims.claim: Most caudal GABAergic PPN neurons (20/22) received inhibitory input from the SNr.
claims.source: We found that all rostral (n=12/12, N=6) and most caudal (n=20/22, N=6) recorded GABAergic PPN neurons received inhibitory input from the SNr (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological recordings showing connectivity between SNr and GABAergic PPN neurons.

claims.claim: The first oIPSC showed no difference between rostral and caudal GABAergic neurons receiving SNr input.
claims.source: The oIPSC amplitudes across the 2 s stimulation as well as the first oIPSC showed no difference between rostral and caudal GABAergic neurons [median (IQR); first oIPSC n=9 Rostral: 76.5 pA (27.0–209.9 pA), n=13 Caudal: 59.7 pA (37.7–269.7 pA); Mann Whitney, U=50, p=0.6005; Figure 3C and D].
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data comparing rostral and caudal GABAergic neurons.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in short-term synaptic plasticity between rostral and caudal GABAergic neurons receiving SNr input.
claims.source: We also did not observe significant differences in short-term synaptic plasticity between rostral and caudal GABAergic neurons [median (IQR); PPR n=9 Rostral: 1.01 (0.88–1.16), n=13 Caudal: 1.06 (0.96–1.15); Mann Whitney, U=48, p=0.5123; Figure 3F and G].
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of paired-pulse ratios from electrophysiological recordings.

claims.claim: The percent inhibition of GABAergic PPN neurons was not significantly different between rostral and caudal neurons during SNr stimulation.
claims.source: The percent inhibition was not significantly different between rostral and caudal neurons (mean ± SEM; %Frequency n=7 Rostral: During Stimulation 37.91 ± 15.91%, Post Stimulation 100.0 ± 14.57%; n=19 Caudal: During Stimulation 30.68 ± 8.03%, Post Stimulation 113.2 ± 5.187%; two-way ANOVA, StimulationF(1, 24)=44.63 p<0.0001, RegionF(1, 24)=0.09642 p=0.7588, InteractionF(1, 24)=0.8841 p=0.3565; Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of firing frequency changes during optogenetic stimulation.

claims.claim: There is a significant negative correlation between PPR and the pre-optical stimulation frequency in GABAergic PPN neurons receiving SNr input.
claims.source: Surprisingly, however, we found a significant negative correlation between PPR and the pre-optical stimulation frequency (Pre-Opto Frq, Figure 3L).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: All rostral glutamatergic PPN neurons (19/19) received inhibitory input from the SNr.
claims.source: Similar to our findings in cholinergic and GABAergic neurons, we found that all rostral (n=19/19, N=6) and all caudal (n=28/28, N=6) recorded glutamatergic neurons received inhibitory input from the SNr (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological recordings showing connectivity between SNr and glutamatergic PPN neurons.

claims.claim: All caudal glutamatergic PPN neurons (28/28) received inhibitory input from the SNr.
claims.source: Similar to our findings in cholinergic and GABAergic neurons, we found that all rostral (n=19/19, N=6) and all caudal (n=28/28, N=6) recorded glutamatergic neurons received inhibitory input from the SNr (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological recordings showing connectivity between SNr and glutamatergic PPN neurons.

claims.claim: The median first oIPSC measured in caudal glutamatergic neurons was significantly larger than those recorded in rostral neurons.
claims.source: The median first oIPSC measured in caudal glutamatergic neurons was also significantly larger than those recorded in rostral neurons [median (IQR); first oIPSC n=13 Rostral: 61.6 pA (19.2–113.9 pA), n=13 Caudal: 313.5 pA (143.8–729.1 pA); Mann Whitney, U=29, p=0.0035; Figure 4D].
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data comparing rostral and caudal glutamatergic neurons.

claims.claim: A 'hotspot' of strong SNr inhibition exists in a medial-caudal group of glutamatergic neurons.
claims.source: After post-hoc staining for the cholinergic PPN and mapping the location of each recorded glutamatergic PPN neuron as described above, we identified a 'hotspot' of strong SNr inhibition in a medial-caudal group of glutamatergic neurons (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on anatomical mapping of recorded neurons combined with electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: The absolute frequency decrease was significantly larger in caudal glutamatergic neurons compared to rostral neurons during SNr stimulation.
claims.source: we found that the absolute frequency decrease was significantly larger in caudal glutamatergic neurons compared to rostral neurons during SNr stimulation [median (IQR); ΔFrq During Opto n=13 Rostral: –3.21 Hz (−12.21 to –1.95 Hz), n=17 Caudal: –14.08 Hz (−20.04 to –6.07 Hz); Mann Whitney, U=55, p=0.0197; Figure 4J].
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of firing frequency changes during optogenetic stimulation.

claims.claim: Caudal glutamatergic neurons fire faster than rostral glutamatergic neurons.
claims.source: We found that caudal glutamatergic neurons fire faster than rostral glutamatergic neurons [median (IQR); Spontaneous Frequency n=11 Rostral: 6.8 Hz (5.4–17.2 Hz), n=16 Caudal: 20.6 Hz (11.2–37.2 Hz); Mann Whitney, U=45, p=0.0343; Figure 4K].
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of spontaneous firing frequencies in glutamatergic PPN neurons.

claims.claim: There is a positive correlation between the PPR and frequency change during stimulation in glutamatergic PPN neurons receiving SNr input.
claims.source: Interestingly, there was a weak but significant positive correlation between the PPR and frequency change during stimulation, showing that input displaying short-term synaptic depression occurs in neurons with greater decreases in firing frequency (Spearman r=0.486, p=0.030; Figure 4M).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: SNr-mediated oIPSCs with larger amplitudes are correlated with greater decreases in firing frequency during stimulation in glutamatergic PPN neurons.
claims.source: As expected, SNr-mediated oIPSCs with larger amplitudes are correlated with greater decreases in firing frequency during stimulation (Spearman r=−0.841, p<0.00001; Figure 4N).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: Greater pre-optical stimulation firing frequency is correlated with larger frequency decreases during stimulation in glutamatergic PPN neurons.
claims.source: Greater pre-optical stimulation firing frequency is correlated with larger frequency decreases during stimulation (Spearman r=−0.791, p<0.0001; Figure 4O).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: Pre-optical stimulation firing frequency is correlated with the first oIPSC amplitude in glutamatergic PPN neurons receiving SNr input.
claims.source: Surprisingly, however, pre-optical stimulation firing frequency is correlated with the first oIPSC amplitude (Spearman r=0.818, p<0.0001; Figure 4P), indicating that the SNr is more strongly connected to glutamatergic PPN neurons with faster firing rates.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: The SNr is more strongly connected to glutamatergic PPN neurons with faster firing rates.
claims.source: Surprisingly, however, pre-optical stimulation firing frequency is correlated with the first oIPSC amplitude (Spearman r=0.818, p<0.0001; Figure 4P), indicating that the SNr is more strongly connected to glutamatergic PPN neurons with faster firing rates.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between firing frequency and synaptic strength.

claims.claim: The median amplitude of the first SNr-mediated oIPSC was the same among rostral PPN neurons irrespective of cell type.
claims.source: We found that the median amplitude of the first SNr-mediated oIPSC was the same among rostral PPN neurons irrespective of cell type [median (IQR); first oIPSC n=15 ChAT+: 74.7 pA (44.5–136.5 pA), n=9 Vgat+: 76.5 pA (27.0–209.9 pA), n=13 Vglut2+: 61.6 pA (19.2–113.9 pA); Kruskal-Wallis, H(2,34)=0.7002 p=0.7046; Figure 5A].
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis comparing SNr input strength across different cell types in the rostral PPN.

claims.claim: The SNr-mediated oIPSCs in caudal glutamatergic neurons were significantly larger than in cholinergic and GABAergic caudal PPN neurons.
claims.source: We found that the SNr-mediated oIPSCs in caudal glutamatergic neurons were significantly larger than in cholinergic and GABAergic caudal PPN neurons [median (IQR); first oIPSC n=20 ChAT+: 109.3 pA (58.5–168.6 pA), n=12 Vgat+: 59.7 pA (37.7–269.7 pA), n=13 Vglut2+: 313.5 pA (143.8–729.1 pA); Kruskal-Wallis, H(2,43)=8.717 p=0.0128; Dunn's test, ChAT +vs Vgat +p = 0.6409, ChAT +vs Vglut2 +p = 0.0042, Vgat +vs Vglut2 +p = 0.0295; Figure 5C].
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis comparing SNr input strength across different cell types in the caudal PPN.

claims.claim: The absolute frequency decrease during stimulation in caudal glutamatergic neurons was larger than both cholinergic and GABAergic neurons.
claims.source: The absolute frequency decrease during stimulation in caudal glutamatergic neurons was larger than both cholinergic and GABAergic neurons [median (IQR); ΔFrq During Opto n=23 ChAT+: –2.10 Hz (−3.11 to –0.84 Hz), n=19 Vgat+: –4.29 Hz (−11.02 to –2.94 Hz), n=17 Vglut2+: –14.08 Hz (−20.04 to –6.07 Hz); Kruskal-Wallis, H(2,56)=24.99 p<0.0001; Dunn's test, ChAT +vs Vgat +p = 0.0049, ChAT +vs Vglut2 +p < 0.0001, Vgat +vs Vglut2 +p = 0.0332; Figure 5D].
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis comparing the impact of SNr stimulation on firing frequency across different cell types in the caudal PPN.

claims.claim: Very few rostral PPN neurons received synaptic input from the GPe.
claims.source: As predicted by the low density of GPe axons present in the rostral PPN (Figure 1D), very few rostral PPN neurons received synaptic input from the GPe.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological recordings showing low connectivity between GPe and rostral PPN neurons, consistent with anatomical observations.

claims.claim: The GPe preferentially targets caudal PPN neurons compared to rostral neurons.
claims.source: These findings show that the GPe preferentially targets caudal PPN neurons compared to rostral neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on connectivity data showing higher percentages of connected caudal neurons compared to rostral neurons.

claims.claim: The percentage of connected caudal neurons was greater than the percentage of connected rostral neurons in both GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons receiving GPe input.
claims.source: The percentage of connected caudal neurons was greater than the percentage of connected rostral neurons in both GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons (one-sided Fisher's exact test; Vgat: OR = 0.2857, CI = 0.09190–0.9391, p=0.047; Vglut2: OR = 0.1637, CI = 0.05069–0.5767, p=0.0033; Figure 6Cii and iii)
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of connectivity proportions between rostral and caudal regions.

claims.claim: The GPe has essentially no direct effect on the cholinergic PPN neural population.
claims.source: These findings indicate that the GPe has essentially no direct effect on the cholinergic PPN neural population.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the observation that GPe-mediated currents in cholinergic neurons were small and had negligible effects on firing frequency.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in the first oIPSC measured in GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons receiving GPe input.
claims.source: While there was no significant difference in the first oIPSC measured in GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons [median (IQR); first oIPSC n=19 Vgat+: 24.77 pA (6.72–54.17 pA), n=15 Vglut2+: 65.71 pA (14.50–133.4 pA); Kruskal-Wallis, H(2,37)=3.050, p=0.2176; Figure 6E]
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data comparing GPe input strength to different cell types.

claims.claim: The GPe-mediated inhibitory input to glutamatergic neurons displayed a significantly lower PPR than to GABAergic neurons.
claims.source: The GPe-mediated inhibitory input to glutamatergic neurons displayed a significantly lower PPR than to GABAergic neurons [median (IQR); PPR n=19 Vgat+: 0.97 (0.76–1.2), n=15 Vglut2+: 0.81 (0.55–0.93); Mann-Whitney, U=76, p=0.0206; Figure 6G].
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of paired-pulse ratios from electrophysiological recordings.

claims.claim: There was no statistical difference between GPe inhibition of firing frequency in caudal GABAergic and glutamatergic PPN neurons.
claims.source: We found no statistical difference between GPe inhibition of firing frequency in caudal GABAergic and glutamatergic PPN neurons
claims.evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of firing frequency changes during GPe stimulation.

claims.claim: Among GABAergic neurons receiving GPe inhibition, the amplitude of the first oIPSC is significantly correlated with the absolute change in frequency during stimulation.
claims.source: Among GABAergic neurons receiving GPe inhibition, we found that the amplitude of the first oIPSC is significantly correlated with the absolute change in frequency during stimulation (Spearman r=−0.627, p=0.044, Figure 6K).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: GPe inhibition of the glutamatergic neurons showed a significant correlation between the absolute change in frequency during stimulation and pre-stimulation firing frequency.
claims.source: GPe inhibition of the glutamatergic neurons showed a significant correlation between the absolute change in frequency during stimulation and pre-stimulation firing frequency (Spearman r=−0.648, p=0.014, Figure 6M).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: Stimulation of SNr axons in the PPN increased distance traveled in the open field.
claims.source: Specifically, stimulation of SNr axons in the PPN increased distance traveled, while stimulation of GPe axons in the PPN decreased distance traveled [mean ± SEM; N=9 (3M, 6 F) Control (Ctrl): 2.22±0.24 m, N=8 (5M, 3 F) SNr: 4.11±0.51 m, N=9 (4M, 5 F) GPe: 0.57±0.18 m; Welch ANOVAW(4.00, 15.86)=14.81, p<0.0001; Dunnett's test, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr4.25mW p=0.0263, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe4.25mW p=0.0002; Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Videos 1 and 2].
claims.evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from open field experiments with optogenetic stimulation.

claims.claim: Stimulation of GPe axons in the PPN decreased distance traveled in the open field.
claims.source: Specifically, stimulation of SNr axons in the PPN increased distance traveled, while stimulation of GPe axons in the PPN decreased distance traveled [mean ± SEM; N=9 (3M, 6 F) Control (Ctrl): 2.22±0.24 m, N=8 (5M, 3 F) SNr: 4.11±0.51 m, N=9 (4M, 5 F) GPe: 0.57±0.18 m; Welch ANOVAW(4.00, 15.86)=14.81, p<0.0001; Dunnett's test, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr4.25mW p=0.0263, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe4.25mW p=0.0002; Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Videos 1 and 2].
claims.evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from open field experiments with optogenetic stimulation.

claims.claim: Mice avoided the stimulated chamber when the SNr axons were stimulated in the RTPP task.
claims.source: Mice avoided the stimulated chamber when the SNr axons were stimulated, but preferred the stimulated chamber when the GPe axons were stimulated (mean ± SEM; N=16 (6M, 10 F) Ctrl: 40.76 ± 2.0%, N=9 (5M, 4 F) SNr: 23.99 ± 5.2%, N=10 (5M, 5 F) GPe: 76.11 ± 3.7%; Welch ANOVAW(4.00,16.95)=26.73, p<0.0001; Dunnett's test, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr4.25mW p=0.0437, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe4.25mW p<0.0001, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr0.25mW p=0.0695, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe0.25mW p=0.0467; Figure 7F, see Videos 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from real-time place preference experiments.

claims.claim: Mice preferred the stimulated chamber when the GPe axons were stimulated in the RTPP task.
claims.source: Mice avoided the stimulated chamber when the SNr axons were stimulated, but preferred the stimulated chamber when the GPe axons were stimulated (mean ± SEM; N=16 (6M, 10 F) Ctrl: 40.76 ± 2.0%, N=9 (5M, 4 F) SNr: 23.99 ± 5.2%, N=10 (5M, 5 F) GPe: 76.11 ± 3.7%; Welch ANOVAW(4.00,16.95)=26.73, p<0.0001; Dunnett's test, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr4.25mW p=0.0437, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe4.25mW p<0.0001, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr0.25mW p=0.0695, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe0.25mW p=0.0467; Figure 7F, see Videos 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from real-time place preference experiments.

claims.claim: The locomotion effect of SNr stimulation over the PPN was no longer present during low power stimulation.
claims.source: We found that the locomotion effect of SNr stimulation over the PPN was no longer present during low power stimulation, but GPe stimulation still significantly decreased locomotion (mean ± SEM; distance traveled N=9 (3M, 6 F) Ctrl: 2.22±0.24 m, N=6 (3M, 3 F) SNr: 2.24±0.50 m, N=8 (4M, 4 F) GPe: 1.09±0.22 m; Welch ANOVAW(4.00, 15.86)=14.81; p<0.0001; Dunnett's test, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr0.25mW p>0.999, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe0.25mW p=0.0131; Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from open field experiments using low laser power to control for antidromic stimulation.

claims.claim: GPe stimulation still significantly decreased locomotion during low power stimulation.
claims.source: We found that the locomotion effect of SNr stimulation over the PPN was no longer present during low power stimulation, but GPe stimulation still significantly decreased locomotion (mean ± SEM; distance traveled N=9 (3M, 6 F) Ctrl: 2.22±0.24 m, N=6 (3M, 3 F) SNr: 2.24±0.50 m, N=8 (4M, 4 F) GPe: 1.09±0.22 m; Welch ANOVAW(4.00, 15.86)=14.81; p<0.0001; Dunnett's test, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr0.25mW p>0.999, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe0.25mW p=0.0131; Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from open field experiments using low laser power to control for antidromic stimulation.

claims.claim: SNr axon stimulation continued to evoke place aversion at the trend level during low power stimulation in the RTPP task.
claims.source: In the RTPP task, SNr axon stimulation continued to evoke place aversion at the trend level and GPe axon stimulation continued to significantly evoke place preference (mean ± SEM; % time in stimulation zone N=16 (6M, 10 F) Ctrl: 40.76 ± 2.1%, N=6 (3M, 3 F) SNr: 27.72 ± 4.0%, N=8 (4M, 4 F) GPe: 68.41 ± 8.5%; Welch ANOVAW(4.00,16.95)=26.73, p<0.0001; Dunnett's test, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr0.25mW p=0.0695, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe0.25mW p=0.0467; Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from RTPP experiments using low laser power.

claims.claim: GPe axon stimulation continued to significantly evoke place preference during low power stimulation in the RTPP task.
claims.source: In the RTPP task, SNr axon stimulation continued to evoke place aversion at the trend level and GPe axon stimulation continued to significantly evoke place preference (mean ± SEM; % time in stimulation zone N=16 (6M, 10 F) Ctrl: 40.76 ± 2.1%, N=6 (3M, 3 F) SNr: 27.72 ± 4.0%, N=8 (4M, 4 F) GPe: 68.41 ± 8.5%; Welch ANOVAW(4.00,16.95)=26.73, p<0.0001; Dunnett's test, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr0.25mW p=0.0695, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe0.25mW p=0.0467; Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from RTPP experiments using low laser power.

claims.claim: Decreased locomotion and place preference are mediated by GPe inhibition of the PPN.
claims.source: These findings show that decreased locomotion and place preference are mediated by GPe inhibition of the PPN, while aversion is mediated by SNr inhibition of the PPN.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data showing that effects persist at low laser power, suggesting local rather than antidromic effects.

claims.claim: Aversion is mediated by SNr inhibition of the PPN.
claims.source: These findings show that decreased locomotion and place preference are mediated by GPe inhibition of the PPN, while aversion is mediated by SNr inhibition of the PPN.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data showing that aversion persists at low laser power, suggesting local rather than antidromic effects.

claims.claim: Selective stimulation of dopaminergic axons in the PPN increased locomotion at high laser power.
claims.source: We found that selective stimulation of dopaminergic axons in the PPN increased locomotion at high laser power (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A) and had no effect on locomotion at low power (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from open field experiments using DAT-cre mice to selectively stimulate dopaminergic neurons.

claims.claim: Selective stimulation of dopaminergic axons in the PPN had no effect on locomotion at low power.
claims.source: We found that selective stimulation of dopaminergic axons in the PPN increased locomotion at high laser power (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A) and had no effect on locomotion at low power (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from open field experiments using DAT-cre mice to selectively stimulate dopaminergic neurons.

claims.claim: Stimulation of dopaminergic axons in the PPN did not cause place aversion, but rather induced real-time place preference at both high and low laser power.
claims.source: On the other hand, we found that stimulation of dopaminergic axons in the PPN did not cause place aversion, but rather induced real-time place preference at both high and low laser power (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from RTPP experiments using DAT-cre mice to selectively stimulate dopaminergic neurons.

claims.claim: The nigral increase in locomotion is not mediated through the PPN.
claims.source: Together, these findings show that the nigral increase in locomotion is not mediated through the PPN, and that dopaminergic input from the SNc to the PPN is rewarding while total input from the substantia nigra to the PPN is aversive.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that dopaminergic stimulation increases locomotion at high but not low power, suggesting effects outside the PPN.

claims.claim: Dopaminergic input from the SNc to the PPN is rewarding.
claims.source: Together, these findings show that the nigral increase in locomotion is not mediated through the PPN, and that dopaminergic input from the SNc to the PPN is rewarding while total input from the substantia nigra to the PPN is aversive.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data showing place preference with dopaminergic stimulation.

claims.claim: Total input from the substantia nigra to the PPN is aversive.
claims.source: Together, these findings show that the nigral increase in locomotion is not mediated through the PPN, and that dopaminergic input from the SNc to the PPN is rewarding while total input from the substantia nigra to the PPN is aversive.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data showing place aversion with non-selective nigral stimulation.

claims.claim: The canonical basal ganglia model predicts that the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) will inhibit locomotion.
claims.source: The canonical basal ganglia model predicts that the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) will inhibit locomotion and the globus pallidus externa (GPe) will enhance it.
claims.evidence: The claim refers to established models in the field of basal ganglia function.

claims.claim: The canonical basal ganglia model predicts that the globus pallidus externa (GPe) will enhance locomotion.
claims.source: The canonical basal ganglia model predicts that the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) will inhibit locomotion and the globus pallidus externa (GPe) will enhance it.
claims.evidence: The claim refers to established models in the field of basal ganglia function.

claims.claim: The GPe exerts non-canonical effects on locomotion through inhibition of the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN).
claims.source: In mice, we use in vivo optogenetics to show that the GPe exerts non-canonical effects on locomotion while the SNr has no gross motor impact through inhibition of the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data showing that GPe stimulation decreases rather than increases locomotion.

claims.claim: The SNr has no gross motor impact through inhibition of the PPN.

results.result: SNr and GPe axons display distinct distribution patterns across the rostral and caudal PPN. SNr axons appear in both rostral and caudal PPN, filling the rostral region evenly but clustering in specific caudal areas. GPe axons densely fill the caudal region while strikingly avoiding the rostral region.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C14 are supported by anatomical observations from confocal imaging (Figure 1B, D) following viral tracing and CUBIC clearing. The qualitative descriptions of axon distribution patterns are consistent with the imaging data presented, though quantitative analysis would strengthen these observations.

results.result: The SNr inhibits cholinergic neurons in both rostral and caudal PPN to a similar extent but evokes stronger rebound firing in rostral neurons. All rostral (19/19) and essentially all caudal (26/27) cholinergic PPN neurons received SNr input with no significant difference in oIPSC amplitude or firing frequency inhibition between regions. However, rostral neurons showed significantly greater rebound activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C22 are well-supported by comprehensive electrophysiological data with appropriate statistical tests (unpaired t-tests, two-way ANOVA, Mann-Whitney tests, correlation analysis). Sample sizes are adequate (n=14-23 cells from N=6 mice), and the findings are internally consistent. The correlation between inhibition and rebound (C22) is weak but statistically significant.

results.result: The SNr inhibits GABAergic neurons in both rostral and caudal PPN to a similar extent. All rostral (12/12) and most caudal (20/22) GABAergic neurons received SNr input with no significant differences in oIPSC amplitude, short-term plasticity, or firing frequency inhibition between regions. A negative correlation between PPR and pre-stimulation frequency suggests functional heterogeneity within the GABAergic population.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C28 are supported by electrophysiological data with appropriate non-parametric statistics (Mann-Whitney tests, two-way ANOVA). The observation of heterogeneity (C28) is interesting and appropriately noted as surprising, suggesting distinct GABAergic subpopulations. Sample sizes are adequate (n=7-19 cells from N=6 mice).

results.result: The SNr differentially inhibits rostral and caudal glutamatergic PPN neurons, with caudal neurons receiving significantly stronger inhibition. All recorded glutamatergic neurons (19/19 rostral, 28/28 caudal) received SNr input, but caudal neurons showed larger oIPSCs, greater firing frequency decreases, and faster spontaneous firing. A medial-caudal 'hotspot' of particularly strong SNr inhibition was identified. The SNr preferentially targets fast-firing glutamatergic neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C39 are strongly supported by comprehensive electrophysiological data with appropriate statistics (Mann-Whitney tests, Spearman correlations). The identification of a 'hotspot' (C32) is supported by anatomical mapping combined with electrophysiology. The correlations (C35-C38) are strong (r values 0.486-0.841) and statistically significant. Sample sizes are adequate (n=11-17 cells from N=6 mice).

results.result: The SNr most strongly inhibits caudal glutamatergic PPN neurons compared to other cell types. In rostral PPN, SNr input strength was similar across all cell types. In caudal PPN, glutamatergic neurons received significantly larger oIPSCs and showed greater firing frequency decreases than cholinergic and GABAergic neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 are supported by comprehensive cross-cell-type comparisons using appropriate non-parametric statistics (Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's post-hoc tests). This analysis effectively synthesizes the previous findings to identify cell-type-specific differences in SNr inhibition strength. Sample sizes are adequate for these comparisons.

results.result: The GPe preferentially but weakly inhibits caudal GABAergic and glutamatergic PPN neurons while largely avoiding cholinergic and rostral neurons. Very few rostral neurons received GPe input across all cell types. In caudal PPN, 68% of GABAergic and 69% of glutamatergic neurons were connected, but only 30% of cholinergic neurons, with negligible functional effects on cholinergic firing. GPe input to glutamatergic neurons showed short-term depression while input to GABAergic neurons showed facilitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C52 are well-supported by electrophysiological data with appropriate statistics (Fisher's exact test for connectivity, Mann-Whitney tests, Kruskal-Wallis, Spearman correlations). The selective avoidance of cholinergic neurons is a key finding. Sample sizes are adequate (n=15-29 cells from N=6 mice). The correlation analyses (C51-C52) provide mechanistic insights into how GPe inhibition affects different cell types.

results.result: In vivo optogenetic activation of GPe and SNr axons in the PPN produces opposing effects on locomotion and valence. At high laser power, SNr stimulation increased locomotion and evoked place aversion, while GPe stimulation decreased locomotion and evoked place preference. At low laser power (controlling for antidromic effects), SNr locomotor effects disappeared but aversion persisted, while GPe effects on both locomotion and preference persisted, indicating these behaviors are mediated by local PPN inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C62 are supported by behavioral data from open field and RTPP experiments with appropriate statistics (Welch ANOVA with Dunnett's post-hoc tests). The low-power control experiments (C57-C60) are critical for ruling out antidromic effects and strengthen the conclusions. Sample sizes are adequate (N=6-16 mice). The opposing effects of SNr and GPe are striking and well-documented.

results.result: Selective stimulation of dopaminergic SNc axons in the PPN reveals distinct effects from total nigral stimulation. Dopaminergic stimulation increased locomotion at high but not low power and induced place preference at both powers, contrasting with the aversion seen with non-selective nigral stimulation. This indicates that nigral locomotor effects are not mediated through the PPN, while dopaminergic input to the PPN is rewarding and total nigral input is aversive.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C68 are supported by behavioral experiments using DAT-cre mice with appropriate statistics (unpaired t-tests). The dissociation between dopaminergic and total nigral effects is important for understanding circuit function. However, the inference that locomotor effects are not mediated through the PPN (C66) relies on the absence of an effect at low power, which could also reflect insufficient stimulation strength. Sample sizes are adequate (N=6-9 mice).

results.result: The study demonstrates non-canonical basal ganglia pathways for locomotion and valence through the PPN. Contrary to canonical models, GPe inhibition of the PPN decreases rather than increases locomotion, while SNr inhibition has no gross motor impact at low power. The structures mediate opposing valence effects, with SNr activation being aversive and GPe activation being rewarding. SNc dopaminergic input to the PPN is also rewarding.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76 represent the main conclusions synthesizing the anatomical, electrophysiological, and behavioral findings. These are well-supported by the comprehensive dataset. The 'non-canonical' designation is justified by the contrast with predictions from classical basal ganglia models (C69-C70). The integration of circuit anatomy with functional outcomes is a strength of the study.

results.result: Prior anatomical and molecular characterization of basal ganglia-PPN connectivity. Previous studies established that SNr and GPe send axonal projections to the PPN, with monosynaptic connections to cholinergic and glutamatergic neurons. The PPN contains three molecularly defined cell types with distinct rostrocaudal topography that is conserved across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C11 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. These provide essential context for the current study. The authors correctly note limitations of prior work, particularly regarding GABAergic neurons (C5-C6) and the lack of regional specificity in previous studies.

results.result: Prior functional characterization of PPN and basal ganglia circuits. Previous studies have implicated the PPN in locomotor control and valence processing, with variable and sometimes contradictory results from optogenetic manipulations. Direct stimulation of molecularly defined SNr and GPe subpopulations produces distinct effects on locomotion and valence. PPN neurons influence dopamine release and connect to reward-related brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C101 provide comprehensive literature context with appropriate citations. The authors accurately characterize the complexity and sometimes contradictory nature of prior findings (C78), which motivates their systematic approach. The discussion appropriately integrates their findings with prior work to explain apparent discrepancies.

results.result: The canonical basal ganglia model predicts that SNr inhibits locomotion while GPe enhances it.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 accurately represent established models in the basal ganglia field. This provides the theoretical framework against which the current findings are evaluated as 'non-canonical.'

results.result: The study characterizes the anatomical distribution of SNr and GPe axonal projections to the PPN along the rostrocaudal axis. SNr axons appear in both rostral and caudal PPN, filling the rostral region evenly but clustering in specific caudal areas. GPe axons densely fill the caudal PPN while strikingly avoiding the rostral region.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm these anatomical findings. Reviewers describe the work as 'carefully dissecting projections' and providing 'important and convincing data on PPN connectivity.' The identification of GPe's selective caudal targeting is noted as 'unexpected and highly relevant' with no concerns raised about the anatomical characterization.

results.result: SNr provides broad inhibitory input to cholinergic PPN neurons across both rostral and caudal regions. Nearly all recorded cholinergic neurons (45/46) responded to SNr stimulation with similar oIPSC amplitudes and paired-pulse ratios between regions. However, rostral cholinergic neurons showed significantly greater rebound activity after inhibition compared to caudal neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the electrophysiological evidence as 'solid' and 'thorough and systematic.' The characterization of SNr effects on cholinergic neurons is accepted as part of the 'prominent influence of SNr across the PPN.' No concerns are raised about these specific findings regarding cholinergic connectivity or regional differences in rebound activity.

results.result: SNr broadly inhibits GABAergic PPN neurons in both rostral (12/12) and caudal (20/22) regions with similar oIPSC amplitudes, short-term plasticity, and percent inhibition between regions. A negative correlation was found between paired-pulse ratio and pre-stimulation firing frequency in these neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the systematic characterization of SNr inputs to different PPN cell types. The evidence is described as 'solid' and part of a 'thorough characterization.' The finding that SNr 'inhibits all major cell types' is explicitly noted by reviewers without challenge to the GABAergic neuron data.

results.result: SNr provides inhibitory input to all recorded glutamatergic PPN neurons (47/47), with significantly stronger inhibition of caudal compared to rostral neurons. A 'hotspot' of particularly strong SNr inhibition was identified in medial-caudal glutamatergic neurons. Caudal glutamatergic neurons fire faster than rostral neurons, and SNr preferentially targets faster-firing glutamatergic neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly highlight that 'SNr projections broadly inhibit all PPN subtypes' and note the study 'stands out for its systematic cell-type-specific approach.' The identification of stronger caudal glutamatergic inhibition is accepted as part of the 'prominent influence of SNr' and the 'anatomical organization' of inhibition. No concerns are raised about these glutamatergic findings.

results.result: Comparing SNr input across PPN cell types, rostral neurons receive similar strength inhibition regardless of neurotransmitter identity. In the caudal PPN, glutamatergic neurons receive significantly stronger SNr inhibition than cholinergic or GABAergic neurons, with correspondingly larger decreases in firing frequency during stimulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the cell-type comparisons as part of the 'systematic' and 'thorough' characterization. The finding that SNr 'most strongly inhibits caudal glutamatergic neurons' is explicitly noted by reviewers as a key result. The evidence is described as 'solid' and 'convincing' with no challenges to these comparative findings.

results.result: GPe shows highly selective connectivity to the PPN, with very few rostral neurons receiving input. GPe preferentially targets caudal GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons while having essentially no direct effect on cholinergic neurons. GPe input to glutamatergic neurons shows greater short-term depression than to GABAergic neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that 'GPe projections are mostly restricted to the caudal PPN and predominantly target glutamatergic neurons, with a lesser effect on GABAergic neurons.' This selective targeting is described as 'unexpected and highly relevant' with the evidence characterized as 'solid' and 'convincing.' No concerns are raised about the GPe connectivity patterns.

results.result: In vivo optogenetic stimulation of SNr and GPe axons in the PPN produces opposing behavioral effects. SNr stimulation increased locomotion and caused place aversion, while GPe stimulation decreased locomotion and induced place preference in real-time place preference tasks.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these behavioral findings, stating the study shows 'convincing evidence that SNr and GPe inputs have opposing effects on behavior.' The results are described as demonstrating 'opposing behavioral effects: SNr stimulation increased locomotion and caused avoidance...while GPe stimulation reduced locomotion and increased time spent in the stimulation zone.' Reviewers note the authors 'addressed key concerns' with additional controls.

results.result: Low-power optogenetic stimulation experiments to control for antidromic effects showed that GPe-mediated locomotor suppression and place preference persist at low power, while SNr locomotor effects disappear but aversion persists at trend level. This suggests GPe effects on locomotion and valence are mediated locally in the PPN, while SNr aversion is also PPN-mediated.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note that 'the potential recruitment of SNc dopaminergic projections was directly tested' and that authors 'addressed key concerns from the initial review by performing new analyses and adding important controls.' The low-power experiments are described as successfully mitigating concerns about antidromic stimulation, with reviewers stating the 'additional controls and thorough discussion now acknowledge and address these caveats appropriately.'

results.result: Selective stimulation of dopaminergic (DAT-Cre) axons in the PPN increased locomotion at high but not low power and induced place preference at both powers. This demonstrates that dopaminergic SNc input to PPN is rewarding, nigral locomotor effects are not PPN-mediated, but total substantia nigra input to PPN is aversive.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that authors 'directly tested using DAT-Cre mice, confirming that dopaminergic axon stimulation drives locomotion and reward but does not explain the aversive effect seen with broader SNr activation.' This control experiment is highlighted as one of the 'important controls' that 'addressed key concerns' and strengthened the conclusions. The dissociation between dopaminergic and total nigral effects is accepted without challenge.

results.result: The study's main conclusions are that GPe exerts non-canonical effects (decreasing rather than increasing locomotion) through PPN inhibition, while SNr has no gross motor impact through the PPN. The two structures mediate opposing valence effects, with SNr causing aversion and GPe causing preference. SNr broadly inhibits all PPN cell types but most strongly targets caudal glutamatergic neurons, while GPe selectively inhibits caudal glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm these main conclusions, describing the study as providing 'a detailed and novel characterization of basal ganglia inputs to the PPN and their behavioral relevance.' The findings are characterized as advancing 'our understanding of how basal ganglia output pathways engage brainstem circuits to modulate locomotion and valence.' Reviewers note the work 'builds on the classic notions of basal ganglia connectivity' and the conclusions are 'significantly improved' after revisions.

results.result: Background claims establishing that SNr and GPe project to PPN with monosynaptic connections to cholinergic and glutamatergic neurons, that PPN has three molecularly defined cell types with distinct rostrocaudal topography conserved across species, and that prior connectivity patterns to GABAergic neurons were incompletely characterized.
results.evaluation: These background claims are citation-based and provide context for the study. Reviewers do not challenge these foundational claims and instead note the study 'builds on' existing knowledge. The characterization of PPN organization is accepted as the basis for the systematic investigation that follows.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on anatomical findings (C12-C14). Both evaluations find the confocal imaging data convincing and support the characterization of GPe's selective caudal targeting. OpenEval notes the qualitative nature and suggests quantitative analysis would strengthen findings, while peer reviewers describe the work as 'carefully dissecting projections' without requesting additional quantification.

Complete agreement on electrophysiological characterization of SNr effects on cholinergic neurons (C15-C22). Both find the evidence solid and systematic with appropriate statistics. OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation while peer reviewers emphasize the thoroughness of the approach. Both accept the weak but significant correlation in C22.

Full concordance on SNr effects on GABAergic neurons (C23-C28). Both evaluations support the findings and note the heterogeneity observation (C28). OpenEval describes it as 'interesting and appropriately noted as surprising,' while peer reviewers accept it as part of the 'thorough characterization' without expressing surprise.

Strong agreement on SNr effects on glutamatergic neurons (C29-C39). Both evaluations support the identification of the caudal 'hotspot' and the strong correlations. OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation (r values 0.486-0.841), while peer reviewers highlight the 'systematic cell-type-specific approach' and accept the anatomical organization of inhibition.

Perfect alignment on cross-cell-type comparisons (C40-C42). Both evaluations find the comparative analysis convincing and well-supported by appropriate statistics. Peer reviewers explicitly note that SNr 'most strongly inhibits caudal glutamatergic neurons' as a key result, matching OpenEval's assessment.

Complete agreement on GPe connectivity patterns (C43-C52). Both evaluations support the selective targeting of glutamatergic neurons and avoidance of cholinergic neurons. Peer reviewers describe this as 'unexpected and highly relevant,' while OpenEval emphasizes it as a 'key finding' with solid statistical support including correlation analyses.

Both support the opposing behavioral effects of SNr and GPe stimulation (C53-C56). OpenEval and peer reviewers find the evidence convincing with appropriate statistics. This pairing covers the primary behavioral findings, while control experiments (C57-C62) are addressed separately.

Partial overlap on behavioral findings. OpenEval R7 covers all behavioral claims (C53-C62) including controls, while peer R8 specifically addresses the low-power control experiments (C57-C62). Both evaluations support these controls as successfully addressing antidromic stimulation concerns, with peer reviewers noting these 'addressed key concerns from initial review.'

Perfect agreement on DAT-cre experiments (C63-C68). Both evaluations support the dissociation between dopaminergic and total nigral effects. OpenEval raises a methodological caveat that absence of effect at low power could reflect insufficient stimulation rather than proving non-mediation through PPN (C66), while peer reviewers accept the conclusions without this qualification.

Complete concordance on main conclusions (C71-C76). Both evaluations strongly support the synthesis of anatomical, electrophysiological, and behavioral findings. OpenEval emphasizes the 'non-canonical' designation is justified by contrast with classical models, while peer reviewers describe the work as 'advancing understanding' and 'building on classic notions' of basal ganglia connectivity.

Full agreement on background literature claims (C1-C11). Both evaluations accept these citation-based claims as accurate context. OpenEval notes the authors 'correctly note limitations of prior work,' while peer reviewers state the study 'builds on' existing knowledge without challenging the background characterization.

OpenEval R11 addresses extensive literature context claims (C77-C101) characterizing complexity and contradictions in prior findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these discussion-section literature claims, though peer reviewers generally affirm the study's integration with prior work.

OpenEval R12 addresses claims about established basal ganglia models (C69-C70) that provide theoretical framework for 'non-canonical' designation. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these model-based claims, though peer reviewers accept the main conclusions that build on this framework.
